old: , because how a change in pCR with exercise translates into fewer recurrences is unknown
para_before: Exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy improves fitness [10–12], and supervised exercise has been delivered during neoadjuvant chemotherapy [16,17], so clinicians can offer it while its effect on recurrence is tested. Trials should record recurrence and follow patients long enough to see whether the effect lasts after the program ends; a higher pCR alone cannot settle the question, because how a change in pCR with exercise translates into fewer recurrences is unknown. Funders can weigh the cost of such trials against the one-year net benefit if an effect is confirmed (Table S9). For payers, the price of a supervised program is far below what a confirmed effect would justify. In Japan, the fee schedule pays for rehabilitation of patients with cancer only during hospital admission, so structured exercise during outpatient neoadjuvant chemotherapy currently has no route to reimbursement [48]. Support that keeps patients exercising after surgery, such as remote programs, would add value if it extends the effect (Table S8). For pembrolizumab, this analysis gives Japan a reference value before any formal evaluation of its perioperative indication.

para_before: The effect of exercise during neoadjuvant chemotherapy on recurrence is unknown, so all results for exercise are conditional on the assumed HR and duration, and the CHALLENGE reference comes from colon cancer. The same HR was applied with and without pembrolizumab, although the effect may differ with immunotherapy, and uptake and adherence were not modeled. Effects on fatigue, quality of life or completion of chemotherapy were not counted, so the maximum affordable cost is likely understated. Survival was modeled from reconstructed data, and the 7-year event-free survival by pCR status came from the conference presentation of the final analysis. Survival after distant recurrence came from a French cohort diagnosed in 2008 to 2020, largely before immunotherapy and antibody–drug conjugates [50]; longer survival with current treatments would raise the costs avoided per prevented recurrence but lower the QALYs gained. Several costs relied on expert input, but no single cost changed the conclusion (Fig. 3), and values from Japanese populations gave nearly the same results as the German value set. Costs borne by patients, such as time and travel, lay outside the payer perspective, and the registry does not capture every case, so the one-year net benefit is likely understated.
para_after: The effect of exercise during neoadjuvant chemotherapy on recurrence is unknown, so all results for exercise are conditional on the assumed HR and duration, and the CHALLENGE reference comes from colon cancer. Effects on fatigue, quality of life or completion of chemotherapy were not counted, so the maximum affordable cost is likely understated. Survival was modeled from reconstructed data, and the 7-year event-free survival by pCR status came from the conference presentation of the final analysis. Survival after distant recurrence came from a French cohort diagnosed in 2008 to 2020, largely before immunotherapy and antibody–drug conjugates [50]; longer survival with current treatments would raise the costs avoided per prevented recurrence but lower the QALYs gained. Several costs relied on expert input and utilities on a German value set, but neither changed the conclusion (Fig. 3; Table S11). Costs borne by patients, such as time and travel, lay outside the payer perspective, and the registry does not capture every case, so the one-year net benefit is likely understated.

para_after: Secondary outcomes were the total costs and QALYs of the four arms and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) between them at recurrence HRs of 0.95, 0.85 and 0.72; the ICER of pembrolizumab against chemotherapy alone; and the exercise effect, as a recurrence HR or an increase in pCR, at which exercise added to chemotherapy alone would gain as many QALYs as pembrolizumab, or the same net monetary benefit, the QALYs gained valued at the threshold minus the incremental cost. Further secondary outcomes were the recurrence HRs at which the maximum affordable cost, or the medical costs avoided, equaled the cost of a program, and the one-year net benefit, the maximum affordable cost minus the program cost summed over eligible patients treated in Japan in one year.

para_before: Exercise cannot replace pembrolizumab in health gained: it would need to lower the recurrence hazard by more than half, far beyond the effects reported in exercise trials [9,14]. In value for money the gap is narrower, because the program costs a small fraction of the pembrolizumab regimen. At the Japanese threshold, exercise added to chemotherapy alone would give the same net benefit as pembrolizumab with an effect the size of that in CHALLENGE, a 28% reduction in the recurrence hazard, and at the higher threshold reserved for designated products pembrolizumab keeps its lead unless exercise cuts the hazard by more than a third. The effect of pembrolizumab is established and that of exercise is not, so a payer choosing one would still choose pembrolizumab; the comparison shows how much health a cheap program could buy if its effect were confirmed.

para_before: The maximum affordable cost was higher without pembrolizumab, because more patients relapse and the same relative effect prevents more recurrences. Pembrolizumab itself was cost-effective in Japan, as in other countries [28–31], and its ICER depended most on its price and on post-operative capecitabine or olaparib as used in Japanese practice.

The effect of exercise during neoadjuvant chemotherapy on recurrence is unknown, so all results for exercise are conditional on the assumed HR and duration, and the CHALLENGE reference comes from colon cancer. The same HR was applied with and without pembrolizumab, although the effect may differ with immunotherapy, and uptake and adherence were not modeled. Effects on fatigue, quality of life or completion of chemotherapy were not counted, so the maximum affordable cost is likely understated. Survival was modeled from reconstructed data, and the 7-year event-free survival by pCR status came from the conference presentation of the final analysis. Survival after distant recurrence came from a French cohort diagnosed in 2008 to 2020, largely before immunotherapy and antibody–drug conjugates [50]; longer survival with current treatments would raise the costs avoided per prevented recurrence but lower the QALYs gained. Several costs relied on expert input and utilities on a German value set, but neither changed the conclusion (Fig. 3; Table S11). Costs borne by patients, such as time and travel, lay outside the payer perspective, and the registry does not capture every case, so the one-year net benefit is likely understated.
